title: 2 Rooks vs 2 Rooks
reviewNotes: Two branches, 13 exact positions from the six-piece post-castling position after ...Rf8 at 77 seconds. Kb1/Ka1 clears b1 for the rook swing and actual Rb8 mate. Immediate Rd6 allows checking activity and draws. Castling rights are a source stipulation and the castling move is outside exact tablebase scope; earlier skewer illustrations remain context.
transcript: Beauty and genius hides in the simplest of positions. Both sides have two rooks left and it seems to be a complete draw. Of course, if we start checking the black king, there is no checkmate. The king can always move away. We can keep giving as many checks as we want. There is no continuation. But white does have an incredible hidden resource in this position that is going to allow him to win. The first thing to notice is that white can still castle in this position. This is the first move of the sequence. First of all, this shields the white king from any rook check and it puts black in a pretty uncomfortable position. If either rook moves away from the last rank, we are going to win some material. For example, if this rook moves here, now there's going to be a skewer. After the king moves, we pick up the rook in the corner. And if this rook moves, there's going to be another check. The king moves and does defend the rook, but we can give another check with this rook and try to get the king away. Of course, moving away would relinquish control of the rook, but the king can step in front of it. Now another check tries to come and pick up the rook from behind. And if black covers, we can take and then take the rook and we win the game. But black can simply wait around with a move like rook to F8 and the question for white becomes, where is the win? You cannot give a ladder checkmate because the king is defending this square. And if you try to prepare a rook swing like this, for example, you now allow black to start checking the white king. And this ends up being yet another draw. But white finds a majestic idea with king to B1. Again, neither of these rooks can leave the last rank, so black has nothing better but to wait around. King to A1. What is possibly the idea here? It's important to notice that the king is blocked by this rook and if it ever comes here, this is going to be a checkmate in just one move. And now, with the king on A1, we have created just enough space for the rook to swing around to B1 and create an unstoppable ladder checkmate threat. The king can try to run this way, but it's one square too far. And so, rook to B8 is going to be a beautiful checkmate. Follow me for more incredible chess.
